title: The mother sauces
intro: Béchamel, velouté, espagnole, tomato and hollandaise, and the small sauces each one gives. Learn the liaison and the liquid of each mother, and the family tree follows.

entries.title: Hollandaise
entries.summary: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction. It is the one mother sauce bound by yolk rather than roux: quick to make, fragile in service and the parent of a whole family.
entries.guest: Hollandaise is a warm butter sauce thickened with egg yolk and brightened with lemon. On the Eggs Hussarde it shares the plate with a red wine sauce.

paras: Hollandaise is a warm emulsion: tiny droplets of butterfat held apart in a little water by the proteins and lecithin of egg yolk. Acid, either lemon juice or a reduction of vinegar and peppercorns, sharpens the flavour and helps the yolk stay smooth under heat. It is the one mother sauce thickened by yolk rather than by roux, which makes it quick, fragile and unforgiving of carelessness.

The name means Dutch sauce, though no clear link to Holland has been found. Kitchens teach it as one of the five mother sauces, a scheme usually traced to Escoffier, and its daughters include béarnaise, mousseline and maltaise.

A dependable working ratio is 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter, about 75 g of butter for each yolk, with 2 tbsp (30 ml) of reduction or lemon juice and a spoonful of water. One yolk can hold far more fat than that, but a sauce pushed to its limit breaks at the first knock, so the ratio buys a margin for service. Clarified butter gives a thicker, steadier sauce; whole butter brings its own water and a softer, milkier taste.

Reduce white wine vinegar with crushed white peppercorns and a little water, strain it and let it cool. Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl set over barely simmering water, never touching it, until they foam and then thicken into a pale ribbon that holds its shape for a moment. The yolks are ready at roughly 65 to 70°C (149 to 158°F); much hotter and their proteins begin to set into curds.

Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time until the sauce takes, then in a thin, steady stream. Season with salt, a squeeze of lemon and a pinch of cayenne. If the sauce stiffens, loosen it with a few drops of warm water: it should coat a spoon and fall from it in a soft ribbon. Strain it, then keep it warm, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie away from direct heat.

A hollandaise fails in two directions. Too hot, and the yolk scrambles into a grainy, curdled sauce. Too cool, or with the butter added too fast, and the fat never disperses, leaving a greasy, split pool. Both are mended the same way: put a spoonful of warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl and whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop. A sauce that has only just turned grainy can sometimes be saved by whisking in a spoonful of cold water off the heat and straining it.

Hollandaise is made in small batches through service rather than held for hours. Warm egg and butter suit bacteria as well as they suit the cook, which is why kitchens make it fresh, hold it warm rather than hot and replace it on a schedule the chef sets. Many kitchens use pasteurised yolks for the same reason.

At Brennan's, hollandaise is the rich, lemony layer on the Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen. Each is paired with marchand de vin, a dark red wine sauce, so the plate carries one bright sauce and one deep one. Describe it to a guest as the classic Benedict sauce, and send any question about what goes into it to the kitchen.

faults.cause: Butter added faster than the yolk could take it, or a base that was too cool.
faults.fix: Whisk a little warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then whisk the split sauce into it drop by drop.

faults.cause: The yolks overheated and began to set.
faults.fix: Off the heat, whisk in a spoonful of cold water and strain; if it has truly scrambled, start again.

faults.cause: Too much butter for the water in the sauce, or held too cool.
faults.fix: Whisk in warm water a few drops at a time until it falls from the spoon in a ribbon.

faults.cause: The yolks were not cooked to a ribbon before the butter went in.
faults.fix: Whisk over gentle heat until it thickens, or start a new yolk and whisk the thin sauce into it.

brennans.how: Hollandaise goes over the poached eggs and coffee-cured Canadian bacon, with marchand de vin beneath, so the plate carries a bright sauce over a deep one.
Over the soft-boiled egg, the red wine braised short rib débris and the Creole-spiced potato, hollandaise brings butter and lemon against the marchand de vin.

cards.front: What kind of sauce is hollandaise?
cards.back: A warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, sharpened with lemon juice or a vinegar reduction.

cards.front: What thickens hollandaise, where most mother sauces use a roux?
cards.back: Egg yolk: its proteins and lecithin hold droplets of butterfat apart in a little water, so no flour is needed.

cards.front: What is a dependable ratio of yolks to clarified butter?
cards.back: About 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter, roughly 75 g a yolk, which leaves a margin for service.

cards.front: How do you know the yolks are ready for the butter?
cards.back: They thicken into a pale ribbon that holds its shape for a moment, at roughly 65 to 70°C (149 to 158°F).

cards.front: What happens when the yolk base gets too hot?
cards.back: The yolk proteins set into curds and the sauce turns grainy; past about 70°C (158°F) the risk climbs fast.

cards.front: How do you rescue a split hollandaise?
cards.back: Whisk a little warm water or a fresh yolk in a clean bowl, then whisk the broken sauce into it drop by drop.

cards.front: Why do many cooks make hollandaise with clarified butter?
cards.back: Clarified butter has had its water and milk solids taken out, so it gives a thicker, steadier sauce than whole butter.

cards.front: How is hollandaise held during service?
cards.back: Warm rather than hot, around 60°C (140°F), in a bain-marie away from direct heat, and made fresh in small batches.

cards.front: Name three sauces built on hollandaise.
cards.back: Béarnaise, with its tarragon reduction; mousseline, with whipped cream folded in; and maltaise, with blood orange.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes carry hollandaise?
cards.back: The Eggs Hussarde and the Eggs Owen, each with marchand de vin, a red wine sauce, alongside it.

questions.q: What holds a hollandaise together, where most mother sauces rely on a roux?
questions.why: The yolk's proteins and lecithin keep droplets of butterfat dispersed in water, so hollandaise needs no starch at all.

questions.q: Which proportion is a dependable working ratio for hollandaise?
questions.answer: 3 yolks to 225 g (8 oz) of clarified butter
distractors: 1 yolk to 500 g (1 lb) of clarified butter
6 yolks to 50 g (2 oz) of clarified butter
3 yolks to 1 litre (4 cups) of warm milk
questions.why: About 75 g of butter a yolk gives a sauce that holds through service; one yolk can take more, but with no margin.

questions.q: At roughly what temperature are the yolks ready to take the butter?
questions.why: The yolks thicken to a ribbon in that window; cooler and they stay thin, hotter and their proteins set into curds.

questions.q: A hollandaise has split into a greasy pool. What is the classic rescue?
questions.answer: Whisk it drop by drop into warm water or a fresh yolk
distractors: Boil it hard until it comes back together
Whisk in a spoonful of flour over high heat
Chill it, then beat in cold butter
questions.why: A fresh base gives the fat something to disperse into, and adding the broken sauce slowly rebuilds the emulsion a droplet at a time.

questions.q: How should a kitchen hold hollandaise through service?
questions.answer: Warm in a bain-marie, made fresh in small batches
distractors: On a direct flame, so it stays hot
In the fridge, rewarmed to order
At room temperature for the whole day
questions.why: Direct heat scrambles it and long warm holding suits bacteria, so kitchens keep it gently warm and replace it often.

questions.q: Which of these sauces is a daughter of hollandaise?
questions.why: Béarnaise is hollandaise built on a vinegar, shallot and tarragon reduction; Mornay and Soubise come from béchamel, and bordelaise from the brown sauces.

questions.q: On which Brennan's dish does hollandaise share the plate with marchand de vin?
questions.why: The Eggs Hussarde, like the Eggs Owen, carries hollandaise with marchand de vin; the Sardou carries Choron instead.

questions.q: Why does clarified butter give a thicker hollandaise than whole butter?
questions.answer: Its water and milk solids have been removed
distractors: It is whipped full of air first
It has been browned to a nutty colour
questions.why: Whole butter brings its own water, which loosens the sauce; clarified butter is almost pure fat, so the same yolks set a thicker emulsion.

entries.title: Béarnaise
entries.summary: Hollandaise built on a sharp reduction of vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon, and finished with fresh herbs. It is the classic sauce for grilled beef and the parent of Choron and Foyot.
entries.guest: Béarnaise is a warm butter and egg yolk sauce sharpened with tarragon and shallot. It is the classic French sauce for steak, and it comes with our hanger steak.

paras: Béarnaise is a warm emulsion of egg yolk and butter, made like hollandaise but flavoured from the start with a reduction of white wine vinegar, dry white wine, shallot, tarragon and crushed peppercorns. Fresh chopped tarragon and chervil go in at the end. The acid and the herbs give it a sharper, greener taste than hollandaise, which is why it stands up to grilled and roast beef.

It is usually credited to the chef Collinet at the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye, west of Paris, in the 1830s, and named for Béarn, the home region of Henri IV. The date, and even the chef's name, are disputed, and some writers find the sauce in print earlier. Its place in the classical repertoire is not in doubt: it is the best known daughter of hollandaise.

For 3 yolks and 225 g (8 oz) of clarified or melted butter, reduce 60 ml (1/4 cup) of white wine vinegar and 60 ml (1/4 cup) of dry white wine with two finely chopped shallots, a few tarragon stalks and a pinch of crushed peppercorns until about 2 tbsp (30 ml) remains. Strain it, or leave the shallot in for a more rustic sauce. The reduction should taste fiercely sharp on its own, because the butter will soften it a great deal.

Whisk the cooled reduction with the yolks over barely simmering water until they thicken to a ribbon, at roughly 65 to 70°C (149 to 158°F), then take the bowl off the heat and whisk in the warm butter, slowly at first. Béarnaise is usually made a little thicker than hollandaise, so it sits on hot meat instead of running off it. Finish with chopped tarragon and chervil, taste for salt and hold it warm in a bain-marie, around 60°C (140°F).

Béarnaise breaks for the same reasons as hollandaise, overheated yolks or butter added too fast, and it mends the same way: whisk it drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk. A sauce that tastes flat usually had a timid reduction, and a few drops of vinegar with more fresh tarragon bring it back. Dried tarragon cannot stand in at the finish, as it gives colour without the fresh herb's anise lift.

Béarnaise has children of its own. Choron folds in tomato purée cooked down to a paste, which turns the sauce a soft coral without thinning it. Foyot, also called Valois, whisks in glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, for a tawny, deeper sauce. Both keep the tarragon.

At Brennan's, béarnaise is printed on the breakfast Creole-Spiced Hanger Steak as French béarnaise, beside a sunny side up egg and a smoked potato pavé. Its daughters work elsewhere on the menu: Choron replaces the usual hollandaise on the Eggs Sardou, and Foyot brings depth to the Roasted Chateaubriand, the leanest cut of the beef carrying the richest sauce.

faults.fix: Whisk it drop by drop into a little warm water or a fresh yolk.

brennans.how: Printed as French béarnaise on the breakfast hanger steak, with a sunny side up Vital Farms egg and a smoked potato pavé.
The Eggs Sardou carries Choron, béarnaise with tomato, over poached eggs, crispy artichokes and Parmesan creamed spinach.
The Roasted Chateaubriand for two comes with sauce Foyot, béarnaise deepened with meat glaze, to give the lean tenderloin richness.

cards.front: What is béarnaise, in one line?
cards.back: Hollandaise built on a reduction of vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon, finished with fresh tarragon and chervil.

cards.front: What goes into a béarnaise reduction?
cards.back: White wine vinegar, dry white wine, chopped shallot, tarragon stalks and crushed peppercorns, reduced to about 2 tbsp (30 ml).

cards.front: Which fresh herbs finish a béarnaise?
cards.back: Chopped tarragon, the defining flavour, and chervil, added at the end so they stay green and bright.

cards.front: How should béarnaise differ in body from hollandaise?
cards.back: It is usually made a little thicker, so it sits on hot meat instead of running off it.

cards.front: Where and when is béarnaise usually said to have been created?
cards.back: At the Pavillon Henri IV in Saint-Germain-en-Laye in the 1830s, credited to the chef Collinet, though the story is disputed.

cards.front: Where does béarnaise take its name from?
cards.back: From Béarn, the region in the south west of France that was home to Henri IV.

cards.front: What is sauce Choron?
cards.back: Béarnaise with tomato purée, cooked down to a paste, folded in, which turns it a soft coral.

cards.front: What is sauce Foyot?
cards.back: Béarnaise with glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze, whisked in for a deeper, tawny sauce; it is also called Valois.

cards.front: Which Brennan's dishes carry béarnaise or its daughters?
cards.back: The breakfast hanger steak carries béarnaise, the Eggs Sardou carries Choron and the Roasted Chateaubriand carries Foyot.

cards.front: How do you lift a béarnaise that tastes flat?
cards.back: Add a few drops of vinegar and more fresh tarragon; a flat sauce usually had a timid reduction.

questions.q: Which herb gives béarnaise its defining flavour?
questions.why: Tarragon goes into the reduction and again, fresh, at the finish; its anise note is what sets béarnaise apart from hollandaise.

questions.q: What is reduced to begin a béarnaise?
questions.answer: Vinegar, white wine, shallot and tarragon
distractors: Red wine, shallot and bone marrow
questions.why: The sharp vinegar and herb reduction is the whole difference between béarnaise and hollandaise; red wine and marrow belong to bordelaise.

questions.q: What turns béarnaise into sauce Choron?
questions.answer: Tomato purée reduced to a paste
questions.why: Choron folds in tomato cooked down thick, so it colours the sauce without thinning it; meat glaze makes Foyot instead.

questions.q: Which addition turns béarnaise into sauce Foyot?
questions.answer: Glace de viande, a reduced meat glaze
distractors: Tomato purée cooked to a paste
questions.why: Foyot, also called Valois, whisks reduced meat glaze into béarnaise for a deeper, tawny sauce suited to lean beef.

questions.q: Compared with hollandaise, how thick is a béarnaise usually made?
questions.answer: A little thicker, so it sits on the meat
distractors: Much thinner, so it can be poured
Thin enough to soak into bread
questions.why: Béarnaise is spooned onto hot grilled meat, so a firmer body keeps it on the steak instead of pooling on the plate.

questions.q: Béarnaise is named for which place?
questions.answer: Béarn, home region of Henri IV
questions.why: The sauce honours Béarn, the region of Henri IV, whose name the Pavillon at Saint-Germain-en-Laye also carried.

questions.q: Which sauce does Brennan's put on the Eggs Sardou?
questions.why: The Sardou swaps the usual hollandaise for Choron, béarnaise with tomato, over poached eggs, artichokes and creamed spinach.

steps.title: Build a hollandaise
steps.prompt: Put the stages of a classic hollandaise in order. One stage does not belong.
steps: Reduce white wine vinegar with crushed peppercorns and a little water, then strain and cool it
Clarify the butter and keep it warm, not hot
Whisk the yolks with the reduction in a bowl over barely simmering water
Keep whisking until the yolks thicken into a pale ribbon
Off the heat, whisk in the warm butter a few drops at a time, then in a thin stream
Season with salt, lemon juice and cayenne, and loosen with warm water if needed
Strain it and hold it warm in a bain-marie, away from direct heat
steps.distractor: Bring the yolks to a rolling boil so they thicken faster
steps.why: The reduction and the clarified butter are ready before the yolks meet any heat; the yolks are taken to a ribbon, and only then does the butter go in, slowly and off the heat.
